passages.happening:
“Then Joseph fell upon his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him” (verse 1).

He tells the physicians in his service to embalm his father, “So they embalmed him, taking the forty days required to complete the embalming. And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days” (verses 2-3).
passages.hearers:
Joseph's first act is not as a ruler but as a son. He falls on his father's face, weeps and kisses him. God had promised Jacob, ‘Joseph's own hands will close your eyes’ (46:4). It has happened.

To embalm a body is to treat it with salts, oils and spices so that it does not decay. Egyptians did this so the body could be kept. Genesis tells of only two embalmings: Jacob's here, and Joseph's own (verse 26). Here it has a practical purpose too: Jacob's body must travel to Canaan.

The numbers need care. Genesis gives forty days for the embalming and seventy days of mourning. Much later, in the 400s BC, the Greek writer Herodotus said that in the costliest Egyptian method a body was laid in natron, a drying salt, for seventy days. The numbers do not match exactly, and practice may well have varied. Many readers take the forty days as the embalming itself and the seventy as the whole time of mourning around it.

What is clear is the honor. The Egyptians mourn this old herder from Canaan for seventy days. Israel later mourned Moses thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8).
passages.later: Jesus wept at the grave of his friend Lazarus: “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). Paul does not tell Christians not to grieve, but “so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
passages.hard: A word of care. Some readers come to this chapter grieving a father or a mother. Joseph's tears were not a lack of faith, and yours are not either. If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Joseph, the second man in Egypt, fell on his father's face and wept. Ask whether you allow yourself to grieve, or whether you think strength means holding it in. Then ask who has stood with you in grief, and who you could stand with.

passages.happening:
After the days of mourning, Joseph asks Pharaoh's court for leave. His father made him swear, “You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan” (verse 5). “Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear to do,” Pharaoh replies (verse 6).

A great procession goes up: Pharaoh's officials, the elders of Egypt, Joseph's household, his brothers and his father's household (verses 7-8). “Chariots and horsemen alike went up with him, and it was an exceedingly large procession” (verse 9).

At the threshing floor of Atad, “across the Jordan”, they mourn seven days (verse 10). The Canaanites see it and say, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians” (verse 11). The place is named Abel-mizraim.

Jacob's sons carry him to the cave at Machpelah and bury him (verses 12-13). Then Joseph returns to Egypt (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Joseph keeps his oath (47:31). He asks Pharaoh politely, through the court, and he promises to come back.

The procession is a state funeral. The highest officials of Egypt walk with a family of shepherds to bury their father in Canaan. Only the children and the flocks stay behind in Goshen.

A threshing floor was a flat, open place where grain was beaten out. It made a good place for a large crowd. ‘Across the Jordan’ is puzzling, since the direct road from Egypt to Hebron does not cross the Jordan. Some think the phrase is said from where the writer stood. Others think the procession took a long way round. No one knows where Atad was.

Abel-mizraim sounds like the Hebrew for ‘mourning of Egypt’. It can also mean ‘meadow of Egypt’. The Canaanites name a place after the grief of foreigners.

And then the burial. Jacob lies in the cave Abraham bought, with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah (49:31). The only land the family owns in Canaan is a grave. Jacob's body there says what he believed: the promise is real. (See the note on 12:4-9 for what the land promise means.)
passages.later: Hebrews says of Abraham's family, “All these people died in faith, without having received the things they were promised. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).
passages.asks: Jacob was carried back to a grave in the land of promise because he believed God's word. Ask what you want your life, and even your death, to say about what you believe. Then ask what promise you are trusting that you have only seen ‘from afar’.

passages.happening:
With their father dead, the brothers are afraid. “What if Joseph bears a grudge? Then he will surely repay us for all the evil that we did to him” (verse 15).

They send a message, saying their father commanded it: “I beg you, please forgive the transgression and sin of your brothers, for they did you wrong” (verse 17). “When their message came to him, Joseph wept” (verse 17).

The brothers come and bow down. “We are your slaves!” they say (verse 18).

“But Joseph replied, ‘Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?’” (verse 19). “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this” (verse 20). That day was “to preserve the lives of many people” (verse 20).

“Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones” (verse 21). He comforts them and speaks kindly to them (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Seventeen years have passed since Joseph first forgave them (45:5; 47:28). Still the brothers are afraid. They think only their father held Joseph back.

Did Jacob really leave that message? Genesis does not record it, and it does not tell us that Jacob ever learned what they did. Many readers think the brothers made it up, or at least shaped it, out of fear. Others say Jacob may well have said something like it in private. The text leaves it open.

Joseph weeps. Perhaps because they still do not trust him.

The brothers fall down and say, ‘We are your slaves.’ It is the last time the dream of chapter 37 comes true. And Joseph comforts them.

‘Am I in the place of God?’ Jacob once said the same words to Rachel, in anger (30:2). Joseph says them in mercy. Judgment and revenge belong to God, not to him.

Then the great sentence of the whole Joseph story. Read it slowly. It does not say that the evil was good. It calls the brothers' act evil: ‘you intended against me for evil’. Two intentions were at work in the same events. The brothers meant harm. God meant good, ‘to preserve the lives of many people’. The evil stays evil. It was not the last word.

And notice who says it. Joseph says it himself, years later, as the one who was wronged. No one says it to him in the pit.
passages.later:
Paul writes, “And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28).

Peter speaks of the cross in the same way: Jesus “was delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death” (Acts 2:23). The church prayed that the rulers who killed Jesus “carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand would happen” (Acts 4:28). As with Joseph, the evil was real, the guilty were guilty, and God meant it for good.
passages.hard:
Genesis 50:20 is a much-loved verse, and an often misused one.

It does not call evil good. It does not say that what the brothers did was all right, or that it did not matter, or that God made them do it. Joseph names it evil.

It is said by the one who was wronged, looking back many years later, when he could see what came of it. It is not something others said to him while he was in the pit, or in chains, or in prison. So it is never a line to hand to someone in fresh grief. And it is never a reason to explain away abuse, or to tell someone who has been hurt that the harm was really good for them. If someone has hurt you, what they did was wrong. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

How does God rule over evil acts without doing evil? Christians answer in more than one way. The Reformed tradition says that God ordains all that comes to pass, even evil acts, without being the author of sin and without taking away human guilt. The Arminian tradition says that God permits evil acts he does not will, gives people real freedom, and then overrules what they do for good. These notes take no side. Both agree on what this verse says: the brothers were guilty, and God's good purpose was not defeated.

The site's Honest Answer, ‘If God is good, why is there so much suffering?’, faces the larger question with care.
passages.asks: Joseph had power over the men who sold him, and he chose to provide for their children. Ask whether there is someone you have forgiven in words but still hold in fear of your revenge. Then ask what it would mean to say to them, in your own way, ‘Do not be afraid.’

passages.t: ‘Carry my bones up from this place’
passages.happening:
Joseph lives in Egypt with his father's household “to the age of 110” (verse 22). “He saw Ephraim's sons to the third generation”, and the children of Manasseh's son Machir were “brought up on Joseph's knees” (verse 23).

“Then Joseph said to his brothers, ‘I am about to die, but God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’” (verse 24).

He makes them take an oath: “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place” (verse 25).

“So Joseph died at the age of 110. And they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
A hundred and ten years was the ideal length of life in Egyptian texts, a mark of a full and blessed life. Joshua also dies at 110 (Joshua 24:29).

Joseph lived in Egypt from seventeen to a hundred and ten, almost his whole life. He was a great man there. But he did not think of Egypt as home.

Twice he says, ‘God will surely visit you’. In Hebrew the verb is doubled for force: God will certainly come and act for you. To ‘visit’ here means to come and take care of his people.

Joseph asks for his bones to be carried up when God brings Israel out. He does not ask to be buried in Canaan at once, as Jacob was. He waits with his people. His coffin stays in Egypt as a promise: one day we are leaving.

So Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt and a promise.

Where does the story go next? Into Exodus. The family grows into a people, a new king arises ‘who did not know Joseph’, and Israel is enslaved. Then God remembers his promise and comes to bring them out. When they go, they carry Joseph's bones.
passages.later:
Exodus begins where Genesis ends: “Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died, but the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly” (Exodus 1:6-7). “Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt” (Exodus 1:8).

God's word to Moses picks up Joseph's very words: “I have surely attended to you and have seen what has been done to you in Egypt” (Exodus 3:16). And when Israel left, “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him” (Exodus 13:19). They were buried at last at Shechem (Joshua 24:32).

Hebrews remembers it as faith: “By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones” (Hebrews 11:22).
passages.asks: Joseph had every honor Egypt could give, and he still asked to be carried home. Ask where you have settled down so comfortably that you have forgotten you are waiting for God to act. Then ask what promise of God you would want carried forward after you are gone.
